justice: The street allocates substantial space to motor traffic with multiple wide travel lanes, while the pedestrian realm appears comparatively narrow and pushed to the edge behind planting strips.

sustainability: The substantial tree planting and continuous vegetated strips contribute to urban greening, carbon uptake, and microclimate regulation.

aesthetics: The boulevard has strong visual order, with symmetrical streetlights, consistent lane markings, and a long, coherent streetscape composition.

Street trees and planted verges soften the wide roadway and improve the overall image quality of the corridor.

walkability: Sidewalks appear to exist on the right side, but they are set back behind planting strips and are not the dominant feature of the corridor.
The road is very wide and no marked pedestrian crossing is visible, which likely makes crossing difficult and reduces route convenience for walkers.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or active frontages directly engaging the sidewalk, limiting pedestrian interest and staying comfort.

The multi-lane, high-speed character of the roadway can discourage less confident cyclists from sharing space with motor vehicles.
The planted edge strips and broad right-of-way suggest there may be room for cycling infrastructure, but it is not legible in the current image.
